newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Attention riveted on payrolls.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Attention riveted on payrolls.

text.p: The fixed-income sector nervously awaited the U.S. March nonfarm payrolls report on Friday morning in search of near-term direction.

Fear of a strong number has weighed on the bond market in recent sessions as players worry the report may contain incipient signs of wage inflation. Economists surveyed by Reuters, on average, expected to see 196,000 jobs created and average hourly earnings rising by 0.4 percent. They also saw the unemployment rate dropping to 5.2 percent from 5.3 percent and average workweek falling to 34.8 hours from 35.0.
The Labor Department was scheduled to release payrolls at 0830 EST/1330 GMT Friday.

"It's become quite perilous (to forecast payrolls) because you never know what people are going to look at," said Chris Rupkey, financial economist at the Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi. "Sometimes they're looking at average hourly earnings and other times at the (overall) number itself."

Rupkey added that the potential for a rally existed as many people may have already discounted a stronger than consensus estimate of new jobs during March. "I have the feeling people are preparing for a worse number," he said.

"If we see 500,000, obviously that's a problem. But 240,000 may not be a shock to the market," Rupkey said. The key to market stability on Friday is that another employment report will appear before the Federal Reserve's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) convenes again on May 20.

Rupkey said the fact that prices held in after a strong report from the National Association of Purchasing Management Tuesday may be an indication the market has oversold and a positive bias may develop.
"We may have exhausted the downtrade for a while. Somehow this data may have been discounted already," said Rupkey.

"There's a school of thought that seasonal factors may not be as aggressive and the number could be lower. But that's not based on the view the economy is slowing," said Dana Johnson, director of research at First National Bank of Chicago. Technical factors such as the large gains seen in construction jobs last month due to warm weather would be responsible.

"For a change the payroll number could be less of an important part of the report than the unemployment rate and average hourly earnings," Johnson said. Unemployment should drop 0.1 percent and a rise of more than 0.4 percent could confirm further tightness in labor markets and wage inflation.

"I don't think the market is as on edge for this report as usual. Even in the bond contracts (futures) implied volatilities are not as high as they usually are," Johnson said. The market knows the Fed will see another payrolls report before May 20 and there's too much other data between now and then, he said.

Economists said if average hourly earnings rose from the 0.2 percent increase seen in February it could drive up the year-on-year increase above the 3.8 percent annualized rate seen recently, and increase worries of rising wage inflation before the next Federal Open Market Commitee meeting.
On Thursday the Fed executed a bill pass to permanently inject reserves into the banking system. Analysts said a coupon pass remained a possibility.

Late Thursday the 30-year Treasury bond was trading at 94-15/32 to yield 7.07 percent. The 10-year was at 95-23/32 to yield 6.85 percent. The five-year was at 99-21/32 to yield 6.71 percent and the two-year was at 99-24/32 to yield 6.39 percent.
Three-month bills were at 5.12 percent; six-month bills at 5.29 percent and year bills at 5.61 percent.
